"Preventative" means: designed or intended to stop something bad from happening before it happens.

That's the heart of it. When something is described as "preventative," its whole purpose is to block a problem in advance — not to deal with the problem after it has already occurred.

Think of it this way: you see a storm coming. You board up your windows before the storm hits. That action is preventative. Compare this to repairing your broken windows after the storm — that is reactive (or remedial). Preventative always comes first, with the goal of making sure the bad thing never happens at all.
The most important contrast to understand

To truly understand "preventative," you must understand what it is not:

  • Preventative = acting before the problem, to stop it from occurring
  • Curative / remedial / reactive = acting after the problem has already happened, to fix it

A vaccine is preventative — you take it when you're completely healthy, so that you don't fall sick later. Taking medicine to cure yourself after you're already sick is the opposite of preventative; it's curative.

This before/after distinction is the single most important thing about this word.
Examples across different areas of life

Health and medicine

This is where "preventative" is used most often. Preventative healthcare means the things you do to avoid getting ill in the first place:

  • Regular health check-ups (so that diseases can be caught early or avoided)
  • Vaccines (so that you don't contract serious illnesses)
  • Eating well, exercising, sleeping enough (so that your body stays strong)

A dentist asking you to floss daily is giving you preventative advice. Drilling and filling a tooth that has already decayed is not preventative — the time for prevention has passed.

Maintenance and machines

Preventative maintenance means servicing something regularly so it doesn't break down. You change the oil in a car not because the engine is already damaged, but so that it doesn't get damaged. An engineer who inspects a bridge every year to catch small cracks before they become dangerous is doing preventative work.

Safety and security

A lock on your front door is a preventative measure — it's there to stop a break-in from happening. A seat belt is preventative — you wear it before an accident, not during or after. Smoke alarms are preventative devices.

Laws and legal systems

You may come across the phrase preventative detention — this refers to holding a person in custody not because they have committed a crime, but because authorities believe they are about to commit one. It is controversial, but the word "preventative" is used here in the same sense: action taken in advance to stop a future harm.

Education and society

Schools sometimes run preventative programs — for example, teaching young students about the dangers of drugs before those students are likely to encounter them. The goal is to prevent the harm before it has a chance to occur.

A few things are always true when this word is used:

  1. There is an anticipated threat or bad outcome. You can only prevent something negative — a disease, a breakdown, an accident, a crime. You don't use "preventative" for neutral or positive events.
  2. Action is taken in advance. The effort happens before the problem, not alongside it or after it.
  3. The goal is to make the problem never happen. Not to manage it, not to reduce its severity after the fact — but to eliminate the possibility of it occurring.
  4. It describes something proactive. A preventative approach involves thinking ahead and acting before you are forced to.

"Preventative" is almost always paired with a noun. Here are the most common pairings you'll see:

  • Preventative measures — steps taken to stop something bad
  • Preventative medicine / healthcare — medicine focused on avoiding illness
  • Preventative action — doing something in advance to stop a problem
  • Preventative maintenance — regular upkeep to avoid breakdowns
  • Preventative care — medical care aimed at keeping you healthy

You will often see the shorter word "preventive" used instead. Both words mean exactly the same thing and are both correct. Preventive is slightly more common in formal writing and medical contexts, but preventative is widely accepted everywhere. If you see "preventive measures" and "preventative measures" used in different places, know that they are interchangeable — there is no difference in meaning.
A simple way to remember it

Whenever you see the word "preventative," ask yourself: Is this action happening before the problem, with the goal of stopping the problem from ever occurring? If yes, the word is being used correctly.

A doctor who gives you a flu shot in October so you don't get the flu in December is being preventative.
A doctor who treats your fever in December after you've already caught the flu is not.

That's the whole word.
